summary: The Kerberos V5 GSS-API mechanism (RFC 4121) hashes channel bindings with MD5. This RFC updates it so the algorithm can be negotiated using the Kerberos crypto framework of RFC 3961, and notes this uses the last extensible field in the client-server exchange.

eli5.summary: Kerberos used one old fingerprint method to tie a login to a connection. This lets it pick a newer, stronger fingerprint method instead.

questions: replace md5 in kerberos channel bindings
how to replace md5 in kerberos gss-api
what is the kerberos exts field
subtitle: Lets the Kerberos GSS-API mechanism tie a login to a connection using a negotiated algorithm instead of MD5.

tldr.problem: The Kerberos V5 GSS-API mechanism computes channel binding verifiers with MD5, which has known weaknesses, and a stronger hash is needed.
tldr.mechanism: Initiators add a channel binding extension in the previously undefined Exts field, holding the output of the Kerberos get_mic operation with key usage number 43, so the algorithm follows from the key's encryption type.
tldr.outcome: New algorithms can be deployed step by step without breaking older implementations. RFC 6542 updates RFC 4121.

today: RFC 6542 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012 that updates RFC 4121. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the MD5 Hash Had to Go
sections.content:
The Kerberos Version 5 GSS-API mechanism in RFC 4121 uses MD5 to compute channel binding verifiers. Because of recently discovered weaknesses in MD5 (see RFC 6151), stronger hash algorithms are needed.

This document updates the mechanism so it can build channel binding information from negotiated algorithms. That lets new algorithms be deployed gradually, without breaking interoperability with older implementations when new attacks appear.
sections.eli5: The old way of making a fingerprint of a connection had cracks in it. This RFC lets people swap in a better fingerprint maker later without breaking old software.

sections.title: The 0x8003 Checksum and the Exts Field
sections.content:
Initiators MUST still fill in the Bnd field so existing acceptors keep working. They MUST also fill in the new extension field, Exts. The RFC uses this field because it is the last extensible field in the Kerberos client-server exchange message, so it defines extensions for future use.

The 0x8003 GSS checksum has the structure of RFC 4121, with Exts now defined at the end. It holds Lgth (octets 0 to 3, currently 16), Bnd (octets 4 to 19), Flags (octets 20 to 23) and the optional delegation fields DlgOpt, Dlgth and Deleg. These last three are present only if GSS_C_DELEG_FLAG is set.

Exts is zero or more extensions. Each has a 32-bit big-endian type, a 32-bit big-endian length in octets, and the data. At most one instance of a given type may appear.
sections.eli5: The old form had an empty box at the end. This RFC says what can go in that box: labelled notes with a type, a size and the contents.

sections.title: The Channel Binding Extension
sections.content:
When channel binding is used, Exts MUST include an extension of type 0x00000000. Its data is the output of the Kerberos get_mic operation from RFC 3961, using key usage number 43, applied to the channel binding data described in RFC 4121 instead of MD5.

The key is the sub-session key from the authenticator if present, otherwise the session key from the ticket. The algorithm is the "required checksum mechanism" for that key's encryption type, so the hash follows from the Kerberos crypto framework.

Initiators unwilling to use an MD5 hash of the channel bindings MUST set the Bnd field to sixteen octets of hex value FF.
sections.eli5: Instead of the old fingerprint, the sender uses the fingerprint method that matches the secret key already in use. A sender who does not trust the old method fills the old slot with all 1s.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
With this mechanism, initiators get no indication whether acceptors check or ignore channel bindings. Whether to enforce channel bindings is up to the application, and RFC 5056 and RFC 5554 give guidance to application developers on channel binding usage.

Initiators must still fill in the old Bnd field to stay interoperable with existing acceptors, which is why the RFC lets them set it to sixteen octets of FF when they do not want MD5 used.
sections.eli5: The sender cannot tell whether the other side actually checks the fingerprint, so programs must decide for themselves whether to insist on it.

sections.title: The Extension Type Registry
sections.content:
IANA created a new top-level registry named "Kerberos V GSS-API Mechanism Parameters", separate from the existing Kerberos parameters registry. Inside it is a sub-registry of extension types, with entries made of Type Number, Type Name, Description and Reference.

It starts with one entry, 0x00000000, "Channel Binding MIC". Types 0x00000000 to 0x000003FF need IETF Review, 0x00000400 to 0xFFFFF3FF need Specification Required, and 0xFFFFF400 to 0xFFFFFFFF are Private Use.
sections.eli5: There is now an official list of note types, and only one is on it so far. Some number ranges need careful review, and some are free for private use.

items.label: Lgth
items.desc: Number of octets in Bnd, little-endian; currently 16.
